## ▶ Offline render path: the fixed cost in the shallow/mid band (2026-08-21)

- [x] ✅⭐⭐**DONE beta.128 — THE SCATTERED-GATHER PASS LANDED; CORRECTION IS NO LONGER THE
  DOMINANT COST.** `fs_iterate_gather` renders a tiny ceil(sqrt(N))-wide texture whose texel *i*
  takes its pixel coordinate from a storage-buffer list instead of from the rasterizer, driving the
  SAME kernel (`iterate_at`, extracted verbatim out of `fs_iterate`) on the same texel-centre
  coordinate. **Measured on this box, same session, A/B against the stashed pre-change build:**

  | scene | correction before | after | whole render |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | loc 03, 1.3e6×, 3,000 it, 1920×1080 | 9.0 s | **0.4 s** (22×) | 11.9 s → 2.4 s |
  | loc 08, 6.6e43×, 60,000 it, mode 2 | — | **0.5 s** | 15.2 s → 2.5 s |
  | loc 07, 1e30×, 600,008 it | (over the gate — fallback) | unchanged | 54.5 s → 53.0 s |

  ⭐⭐**OUTPUT IS BYTE-IDENTICAL.** Decoded-RGB A/B at all three locations: **maxD 0**, and
  `refs=64 residual=69` at loc 03 matches the pre-change run exactly. The corrector still repairs
  precisely the **197 px** it always did (measured against `--no-glitch`), so it has not quietly
  stopped correcting. Gates: selftest **131/131** + goldens 17/17, F3 corpus **20/20 maxD 0**,
  workspace 234, `cargo check` zero-warning.
  ⭐**Two things to carry forward:**
  • **The per-call shader compile had to be hoisted too — and the old refutation was REGIME-BOUND.**
  "Cache the ShaderModule + pipelines" was measured false at 12 ms of a 138 ms pass — 8%. Once the
  gather turned the pass into a **3 ms** dispatch, that same 11 ms became the largest single cost in
  the loop (63 × 11 ms ≈ 0.7 s of a 1.3 s correction); hoisting it into a lazily-built `GatherPass`
  took correction 1.3 s → 0.4 s. ⭐**A cost measured as a FRACTION expires the moment its
  denominator moves** — re-measure every "too small to matter" after the thing it was small
  compared to shrinks.
  • **The gather cannot bound its own dispatch length.** A batch is a handful of pixels, so its wall
  is one pixel's entire dependent chain and no batch size shortens it — whereas a tile splits along
  the ITERATION axis. `gather_dispatch_safe` therefore gates on exactly the question
  `ChunkPricer::open` already answers for a tile (`max_iter <= 400,000`), and above it the beta.127
  tiled + ROI path stays as the fallback — which is why loc 07 is unchanged. The batch size is
  deliberately FIXED for the same reason: `export_tile_cap` is an AREA actuator, and halving a
  latency-bound batch leaves the wall alone while doubling the batch COUNT — applied repeatedly that
  rebuilds the >1 h pathology. `max_dispatch_ms` is now carried out of the correction loop (it used
  to be discarded, so a corrected export logged `max_dispatch=0ms` whatever it had just done): it
  reads 53 ms at loc 03 and 9 ms at loc 07, so the 400k gate is conservative by a wide margin and a
  later slice can raise it ON EVIDENCE.
  ⚠**Left open by this**: (a) a `fs_iterate_chunk_gather` on the iteration axis would extend the win
  past 400,000 iterations, where correction is still 48.6 s at loc 07; (b) ⚠the F3 corpus stages
  `glitch_correct = false` (`validation/corpus/session-template.toml:108`), so it gates the shared
  kernel but **not the corrector** — the A/B above is the only evidence for that, and the new
  selftest check "scattered-gather iterate is bit-identical" the only automated one; (c) `perf.jsonl`
  still reads `gpu_iterate=0.0ms` on corrected exports (`render_iter_tiled` hard-codes it).
  Original item:

- [x] ~~🟠⭐**THE CORRECTION LOOP DOMINATES, AND THE FIX IS A SCATTERED-GATHER PASS.**
  ⭐⭐**MEASURED 2026-08-21** (`FRACTADYNE_TRACE=glitch`, not inferred):
  • **1.3e6×, 3,000 iter, 1920×1080: correction is 10.2 s of an 11.1 s render**, runs the full
  64 references, and STILL leaves 69 glitched pixels. Per-pass: 489→415→386→365→362→359→358…
  — passes 5..64 re-iterate all 2,073,600 pixels to resolve ONE OR TWO.
  • **4.6e1105×: correction is 104 s of a 153 s render**, 455⇒91 residual.
  ⛔**A diminishing-returns stop is NOT a free win** — pass 15 resolved **52** after ten passes
  resolving 1–5 each, so "stop when a pass stops paying" quits early and loses real corrections.
  Progress is NOT monotone. Any early-stop is a QUALITY TRADE and needs the user's call.
  ⛔Zero-progress stopping is exact but never fires here (min observed resolve = 1/pass).
  ✅**Partially addressed beta.127 `48d34ea`** — correction passes now skip tiles with no
  glitched pixels (`render_iter_tiled(.., roi)`). Two currencies, because the loop ends on
  whichever bound it hits first: max_refs-bound (1.3e6×) got 10.2⇒9.0 s at byte-identical
  output; deadline-bound (4.6e1105×) got 57 passes where 37 fit, residual 122⇒91 — the wall
  did NOT drop, because the surviving tiles carry nearly all the cost (non-uniform tile cost,
  same lesson as the 5K loss). ⚠Tile granularity is the ceiling here: at 3,000 iter the tiles
  are 816 px, so scattered glitches touch 10 of 11 tiles.
  ⭐⭐**THE REAL FIX — a GATHER pass, no quality trade at all.** Correction wants "iterate exactly
  these N pixels", and N is a few hundred out of 2M. Pack the glitched pixel coordinates into a
  storage buffer, render a tiny W×H texture (489 px → 32×16) whose texel i takes its pixel
  coordinate from `coords[i]` instead of `px_offset + frag.xy`, then scatter the results back.
  That is ~4,000× less work per pass with IDENTICAL output and no policy decision — it would
  make correction essentially free at any depth, removing 9 s from the shallow band and 100 s
  from the extreme one. Cost: one new fragment entry point (the existing `fs_iterate` body with
  a coordinate indirection) + a coords binding + a scatter on readback. This supersedes the
  early-stop debate entirely.
  ⛔⛔**TWO PLAUSIBLE FIXES MEASURED FALSE 2026-08-21 — do not retry them:**
  • **"Cache the shader module + pipelines per device."** `render_iter_tiled` does rebuild them
  every call, but timed: **setup is 12 ms of a 138 ms pass — 8%.** wgpu/naga already absorb it.
  Caching cannot pay for more than a twelfth of this.
  • **"Shrink the tile when an ROI is set, so skipping actually excludes area."** Tried at 128 px
  (from 816 px): skipping did improve (1/11 → 58/155 tiles) and output stayed byte-identical, but
  correction got **SLOWER — 138 → 161 ms/pass, 9.0 → 10.6 s.** Per-tile FIXED overhead dominates,
  not bytes moved. Comment left in `export.rs` at the tile-size computation so it is not retried.
  ⇒ What remains in a pass: ~11 tile dispatches each allocating two full RGBA32F textures plus a
  same-sized readback, i.e. ~33 MB of allocate-copy-map per pass to repair a handful of pixels.
  **Only the gather pass removes both the per-dispatch overhead AND the readback** (one small
  dispatch, 2 KB back instead of 33 MB). That is now the ONLY identified fix, not merely the best.
  (c) minor, still true: `current_export_request_for` is called THREE times per render
  (`main.rs` ≈ 3995, `render.rs` ≈ 2020, ≈ 2205), each re-scoring 101 reference candidates.
  ✅**"Is it just OVER-DETECTION?" ANSWERED — no.** 489 pixels are flagged at 1.3e6× but the
  corrected and `--no-glitch` renders differ in **197 pixels with a mean colour delta of 224**
  (max 250) — real, visibly-wrong pixels, not false positives. Detection is ~2.5× conservative,
  which is harmless. ⭐So the economics are settled: **0.7 s uncorrected vs 9.9 s corrected, to
  repair 197 px of 2,073,600.** Correction is NECESSARY and its implementation is ~4,000× more
  expensive than the work it does.
  ⚠**Instrumentation traps**: `--profile` calls `render_export` DIRECTLY and cannot see this
  path at all — which is why profiling always looked healthy while `--render` took 11 s. And
  `perf.jsonl` reads `gpu_iterate=0.0ms ~0.00 Gsteps/s` on every corrected or normalized export
  because `render_iter_tiled` hard-codes `iterate_ms: 0.0`. Fix that too, or the next person
  re-derives all of this.

  reports ~11 s of RENDER time against <0.1 s of nominal GPU work, and the cost is nearly

  `--render` does NOT use `render_export`: with `glitch_correct` on (the default) and
  `--normalize` off it takes `render_export_corrected` → `render_corrected_iter`, whose loop
  (`render.rs` ≈ 2052–2161) runs up to **64 full-frame passes** and stops only when the
  glitched set is EXACTLY EMPTY, the 64-ref cap is hit, or the 120 s deadline expires. A
  handful of permanently-unresolvable pixels therefore buys 63 more full-frame passes that fix
  nothing. ⭐**The clincher**: scene 10 enters the SAME entry point and finishes the whole
  base pass in 233 ms — because Direct mode hits the `is_direct()` early return and skips the
  loop entirely. Same path, loop skipped, 47× faster.
  **Per-pass fixed costs, none scaling with iterations**: (a) `shader_module()` +
  `fullscreen_pipeline()` are rebuilt on EVERY call (`lib.rs` ≈ 564/590) — naga parse +
  validate + driver compile of a 121 KB shader, per correction pass; the doc comment there
  explicitly assumes "each export builds it once", which 64 passes violates. This is the same
  shape as the beta.126 lazy-chunker fix, one level up. (b) a fresh bignum reference + BLA tree
  per pass. (c) three full-frame CPU scans per pass. (d) `current_export_request_for` is called
  THREE times per render (`main.rs` ≈ 3995, `render.rs` ≈ 2020, ≈ 2205), each re-scoring 101
  reference candidates.
  **Fixes, in impact order**: (1) bound the loop by BENEFIT — stop when a pass resolves <~0.1%
  of the glitch set, and give the offline path a wall budget far under 120 s; (2) cache
  `ShaderModule` + pipelines per device; (3) hoist the duplicate request builds.
  (Reproduce with `FRACTADYNE_TRACE=glitch`; A/B with `--no-glitch`.)~~
  ⚠**Instrumentation trap**: `--profile` calls `render_export` DIRECTLY and therefore cannot
  see this path at all — which is why profiling has always looked healthy while `--render`
  took 11 s. And `perf.jsonl` reads `gpu_iterate=0.0ms ~0.00 Gsteps/s` on every corrected or
  normalized export because `render_iter_tiled` hard-codes `iterate_ms: 0.0`. Fix that too, or
  the next person re-derives all of this.~~

- [x] ✅**DONE 2026-08-21 — audit of the `+∞` magnification demotion window.** ⭐**F3 corpus
  gate re-run on beta.126: 20/20 MATCH, maxΔ 0 on every location**, including all five past

Goal restated by the user: a release **stable enough to announce publicly**, meaning (a) no easily
reproducible bugs, (b) no fundamentally missing features, (c) something substantively new in the
landscape, and (d) a runnable Linux build. Head is **v0.2.40-beta.50**, pushed; the latest

device loss + black deep holds resolved (beta.49/50, livetest baseline all-green); A1's remaining
half (explicit iteration count still capped live) and the A4 ghost are what is left. Windows is
stable enough that **B (Linux) is unblocked** per the user's sequencing.

### B — BLOCKERS: runnable Linux build (d)

5. **Release artifacts — ✅DONE 2026-08-10**: `release.yml` gained a `linux` job (ubuntu-22.04,
   tar.gz + sha256, uploads to the same release with retry-for-race; manual runs upload an
   artifact). ✅**Proven 2026-08-15** on `v0.2.40-beta.104`: the never-run `linux` job worked
   first try (13.7 MB tar.gz + sha256).
   ⭐**The retry-for-race was a real defect, fixed 2026-08-15.** Only the `windows` job called
   `gh release create`; `linux` uploaded into whatever that job had made, retrying 6×30 s if it
   was not there yet. Linux builds FASTER, so it always spent part of that budget waiting on
   Windows — it fit on beta.104, but a slow Windows build would have exhausted the retries and
   published a release **silently missing the Linux asset**. Restructured into a fan-out/fan-in:
   a `create-release` job makes a **draft** first, `windows` and `linux` upload into it in
   parallel with no retry loop, and a `publish` job undrafts it only after BOTH succeed. A failed
   build now leaves an unpublished draft (invisible to `--check-updates`) instead of a
   half-populated release. Manual runs skip both new jobs, so the build jobs must treat a
   *skipped* `create-release` as a go — hence the `!cancelled() && (success || skipped)` guard.
   ⭐**Second defect found while reading it**: the `linux` Package step never copied
   `validation/golden/BLESSED-GPU.txt`, which `windows` has always shipped. An absent marker means
   STRICT golden comparison (beta.93), so **every Linux tester on a non-3080 card would have seen
   expected cross-vendor variance reported as self-test failures** — exactly the confusion the
   tolerance was built to prevent. The beta.104 Linux tarball on the shelf has this flaw; it is
   cosmetic (strict is the safe direction — it over-reports, never under-reports) but it wastes
   the feature for precisely the audience it was written for. ⚠Both fixes are **untested until
   the next tag** — workflows fire only at the user's request.

    `f32: From<f64>` is not satisfied"* (rust#154024). All 31 were the same shape — an unsuffixed
    float literal as the generic `Into<f32>` width argument of `egui::Stroke::new` — across

    `cargo fix`: 31 insertions, 31 deletions, every one just the literal plus `_f32`. **Provably
    semantics-free** — the literals were already inferring to `f32`; the lint objects to the
    inference *path*, not the result. Four further warnings, visible only under `--all-targets`
    and predating the bump, were cleared at the same time so the baseline holds under both
    invocations: an unused row index in a deliberately row-invariant dither-test ramp, and the

    warnings): the bump also added `manual_is_multiple_of`, `items after a test module`, and
    `unnecessary_unwrap` to the set surveyed here. The `unnecessary_unwrap` was checked and is not
    a bug — the `unwrap()` is in the `else` of its own `is_none()` guard. Left as-is, consistent
    with this item's original finding that the residue is intentional or cosmetic.

      temporal bisection exactly as specced below (`progressive_frame_order`, permutation-pinned
      by unit test; smoke: grand tour 34/34 frames, write order = keyframe seed pass then gap
      bisection, `--resume`/mp4/status-marker unchanged). Normalize caveat handled as a warning
      (palette EMA follows render order — sequential recommended for final normalized delivery;
      time-keyed normalize ranges would lift this, noted as a possible follow-up).
      **Progressive (preview-first) render order** (user, 2026-08-11). Today a tour renders frame
      0, 1, 2, … in order, so you don't see how the *end* of the tour looks until the whole thing
      is done — an expensive way to discover that a deep keyframe is mis-framed or the palette
      drifts. Add a **render-order option** so a "preview-first" pass renders the keyframes first,
      then repeatedly **bisects the largest unrendered gap** between already-rendered frames until
      every frame exists. The result is a coarse flip-book of the *entire* timeline within seconds,
      refining to full temporal resolution — you can eyeball the whole arc and stop/redo before
      committing the full render.
      - **Name.** Recommend **"Progressive"** as the user-facing render-order label (vs the
        default **"Sequential"**), with a subtitle like *"preview the whole tour first, refine to
        full detail"*. The underlying schedule is a **temporal bisection** (a.k.a. binary
        subdivision / interleaved order) — the same idea as a progressive/interlaced JPEG, applied
        to the time axis rather than scanlines. ("Interleaved" and "coarse-to-fine" are accurate
        alternates; "Progressive" reads most clearly to a non-specialist.)
      - **Scheduling.** Emit frame indices as: all keyframe times (snapped to frame indices),
        then a max-gap bisection queue (repeatedly split the widest rendered-neighbour interval at
        its midpoint). Naturally yields the powers-of-two refinement (½, ¼+¾, ⅛…) between each
        keyframe pair.
      - **Muxing caveat.** The out-of-order frames must still be written to their correct
        `frame_%05d` indices on disk; the preview is browsed as stills (or a low-fps proxy) —
        MP4 assembly still happens once at the end from the completed, in-order set. If a partial
        stop is allowed, a "preview proxy" MP4 could be assembled from whatever's rendered so far
        by holding each frame until its next rendered successor (nearest-rendered hold).
      - **Interlocks.** Reuses the resumable-render machinery (already skips frames present on
        disk) and the per-keyframe budgets; independent of the per-frame cost/memory bounds
        (Open bugs) since it only reorders *which* frame renders when, not how each is costed.

### T — Testing gaps (external review 2026-08-13, evaluated + sequenced)

The review's frame: strong at the integration level (F3 corpus = cross-implementation oracle to
4.6e1105×, livetest live-vs-truth with drift baselines, `--uitest`/`--juliadive` scenario
harnesses, bench-matrix determinism), thin at the unit/property level — and structurally blind
to HARDWARE VARIANCE (everything blessed on one RTX 3080). Sequenced by announce value:

1. [x] ✅**DONE — (a) beta.89–92, (b) beta.93.** (a) `--gputest` ships and answered the question it
   was built for: NVIDIA folds the error-free transforms on all three backends, AMD's Vulkan/GL
   preserve them, AMD's DX12 fails differently again. (b) Goldens now carry a **cross-GPU
   tolerance**: `validation/golden/BLESSED-GPU.txt` records the blessing card, and on any other
   card the comparison uses meanΔ alone against 24.0 — calibrated from the RX 6800 XT's real
   spread (≤0.1 on seven goldens, 0.5–0.9 on five, 2.8–4.6 on three, 19.15/16.51 on the two deep
   multibrots) and far below a structurally wrong render (100+). maxΔ is deliberately ignored
   off-reference: one iteration either side of an escape boundary lands anywhere in a cycling
   palette, so it saturates at 255 on a healthy image. ⚠An ABSENT marker means STRICT — a missing
   file must never silently loosen the release gate.
   **Shader-vs-oracle primitive harness + golden tolerance mode** — the B6/hardware pair.
   (a) A dev harness (e.g. `--gputest`) evaluates the WGSL df32/floatexp primitives (add, mul,
   square, split/renorm, the floatexp exponent ops) on chosen inputs — including the regimes the
   17 goldens never visit — against the CPU implementations, reporting per-op max error. This is
   the tool that would LOCALIZE the open 3080-vs-3070 deep-view divergence instead of inferring
   it from screenshots. (b) Goldens gain a TOLERANCE mode for non-reference GPUs (exact match
   stays for the blessed 3080): cross-vendor FMA contraction/rounding legitimately differ, so
   exact-elsewhere would cry wolf and mask real breaks. Together these make "run the self-test
   on your GPU" (the Diagnostics dialog plan) meaningful on stranger hardware.
2. [x] **Parser panic-fuzz extension** — DONE beta.89. `.kfr` (`fuzz_parse_kfr_panic_free`) and
   the `.fdn` value chain (`fuzz_metadata_parser_panic_free`) were already covered; the hole was
   the tour-TOML read/resolve path, now fuzzed two ways (`fuzz_parse_tour_text_panic_free`:
   random grammar tokens, plus byte mutation of a VALID script so it reaches deserialize +
   cross-reference resolve — random bytes never get that far). No panic found in 8,000 samples.
   ⭐**But reading the path for the fuzz found a real one**: an unbounded `zoom` exponent sized
   `precision_for_octaves`, so `zoom = "1e1e999"` saturated the octave cast and asked astro-float
   for a usize::MAX-bit BigFloat — death by allocation on opening a shared file. Bounded in
   `parse_zoom_log10` (ceiling 1e1000000×, ~1000× past the deepest verified corpus location);
   all nine shipped tours unchanged, hostile shapes pinned by test. ⚠Lesson: `.fdn` already had
   `MAX_LOAD_OCTAVES` clamping with a "memory DoS" comment — the guard existed, the newer format
   just never got it. **Worth auditing the remaining untrusted entry points for the same
   asymmetry** rather than assuming the pattern was applied uniformly.
3. [x] ✅**Export writer unit tests — DONE 2026-08-15 (beta.104).** 16 tests, no GPU, ~0.1 s:
   10 in `fractadyne-export` (`writer_roundtrip_tests`) and 6 in `scripting.rs`
   (`resume_vetting_tests`). What they pin, chosen as properties the app depends on rather than
   "it runs": the PNG bytes are EXACTLY `to_srgb8_dithered` of the buffer (the identity every
   golden comparison rests on — if it drifts, every golden fails for a reason unrelated to
   rendering); `write_png_rgba8` does not re-encode already-display-space pixels (the double-encode
   it exists to prevent); metadata round-trips verbatim through both PNG `tEXt` and the EXR
   attribute, with absence reading as `None` rather than `""`; EXR is linear RGB with alpha passed
   through untransformed; a short buffer is refused AND leaves no file behind for `--resume` to
   mistake for a finished frame; corrupt input is a typed error, never a panic.
   ⭐**A real finding, and the tests now pin it in BOTH crates**: the PNG decoder accepts a file
   truncated by ONE byte — IEND's final CRC, which it never verifies — while rejecting the loss of
   the whole IEND chunk. That is exactly the shape an interrupted write leaves, and it is precisely
   why `png_frame_size` tests for the 12-byte terminator ITSELF instead of trusting a successful
   decode. The vetter's test writes that one-byte-short frame and asserts it is discarded; the
   export test asserts the decoder accepts it, with each pointing at the other. Two of my
   assumptions about which truncations decode were wrong before measuring — the tests record what
   the decoder DOES.
   Original: the byte-level writers have zero direct coverage (the goldens exercise the pipeline
   incidentally, end-to-end): PNG encode + metadata embed → read-back roundtrip (pixels AND
   metadata), EXR write/read, the resume-vetting reader. Pure functions, no GPU, half a day;
   corruption there eats user work silently.
4. [x] **Property tests on the pure functions** — DONE beta.105 `bd34ece`. 11 tests, ~24k
   generated cases: `progressive_frame_order` (exact permutation over random ranges incl.
   reversed endpoints and out-of-range seeds; order depends only on the in-range seed SET;
   every seed leads in time order), `segment_range` (tiles [0,F) with no gap/overlap; index
   clamps; 0 segments = 1; more shards than frames still tiles; multiply safe below ~2.9e17
   frames), `budget_step` (never 0 and never above ceiling; a lethal reading never asks for
   more work; NaN/inf/negative frame times cannot wedge it).
   NO dev-dependency was added — a hand-rolled deterministic xorshift64* gives reproducible
   failures and keeps the workspace's zero-dev-dependency property. Two habits worth copying:
   the randomized sweeps carry **anti-vacuity counters** (`budget_step` returns an Option, so a
   change that made it decline most readings would leave every assertion unexecuted and the test
   green), and both suites were **mutation-checked** — `end += 1` in `segment_range` fails 4 of 5
   tests naming the case, dropping the `TDR_MIN_STEPS` floor fails 4 controller tests.
   ⚠`segment_range` had NO tests before this, despite being what shards a render across machines.
5. [~] **Coverage measurement** as a local script — `scripts/coverage.ps1` LANDED beta.105;
   coverage itself is still UNMEASURED because the prerequisites are not installed on this box and
   installing them was not done unasked (`rustup component add llvm-tools-preview` +
   `cargo install cargo-llvm-cov`; a `rustup toolchain install` in this repo already moved a
   compiler version and added 31 warnings unasked, so the script probes and instructs instead,
   or installs on an explicit `-Install`). Verified: ASCII-only, parses under Windows PowerShell
   5.1, and the missing-prereq path exits 2 having changed nothing.
   ⭐Design point worth keeping: a bare `cargo llvm-cov test` UNDERSTATES this project badly —
   `cargo test` reaches the pure logic only, while every GPU path lives in `--selftest` (121
   checks + 17 goldens) and `--livetest`, which run as the BUILT BINARY and are invisible to it.
   A tests-only number would argue for unit tests duplicating what the harnesses already prove.
   So the script runs each phase with `--no-report` and merges one report at the end; `-TestsOnly`
   exists but says loudly that it covers pure logic only.
   Remaining: run it (needs the two installs), then read the report and file what it exposes.
   Deprioritized: egui_kittest widget tests (highest cost; the scenario harnesses have caught
   the recent UI bugs faster than widget-level tests would have).
6. [ ] ⭐**Automate test runs on the remote GPU machines (user, 2026-08-16).** Today every
   cross-machine run is hand-driven: pull, rebuild, run the script, copy results to the share, ask
   for them to be read. That loop cost real time on 2026-08-16 — one six-phase run was started **53
   seconds** after the fix it was meant to exercise was pushed, so it measured the previous binary
   and nobody could tell until the logs were read against the commit timestamp.
   **Topology already in place**: `D:\share` is a local directory on the dev box published as SMB
   share `share`; the Radeon box mounts it and writes reports in. So a bidirectional channel exists
   with no new credentials.
   ⚠**Remoting alone does NOT solve this, and the reason is the whole design constraint.** WinRM and
   SSH sessions on Windows are non-interactive: an eframe/wgpu app there usually cannot create a
   swapchain, and where it can it may land on a software adapter — GPU timings that look plausible
   and describe nothing. Fine for the headless phases (`--selftest`, `--gputest`, the offline
   torture lane), useless for `--play`/`--livetest`, which are exactly the ones that matter for the
   device-loss class.
   **Proposed shape**: a watcher running in the LOGGED-ON desktop session on each test box, polling
   `<share>/Fractadyne/jobs/`. The dev side drops a job file; the watcher pulls, rebuilds, runs, and
   writes results back. Because it lives in the user's session it has the real desktop and the real
   GPU, and being a separate process it survives the device losses under investigation.
   - ⚠**Job files must carry PARAMETERS, not commands** — a phase list, `--set` overrides, env flags
     — with the watcher only ever invoking a whitelisted script. A watcher that executes arbitrary
     strings off a network share is a remote-execution backdoor on the test box.
   - Must record the **commit SHA actually built** in the results, so "did this binary contain the
     fix?" stops being inferred from log timestamps. That single field would have saved the wasted
     run above.
   - Alternative if remoting is preferred: `schtasks /run /s <host> /tn <task>` against a task set
     to *"run only when user is logged on"* launches into the interactive session and keeps GPU
     access — but needs the task defined up front plus credentials/domain trust, and gives less
     control over parameters.
   Applies to the Linux rig too; `scripts/pull-linux-reports.ps1` already establishes the scp/ssh
   half of the same idea.

### E — (b) fundamentally missing features: assessed, nothing blocking

Nothing *fundamental* is absent for a deep-zoom explorer. The honest gaps, all defensible to name
in the post rather than fix: no custom-formula scripting (Ultra Fractal's domain), no layers/blend
compositing, exports capped at the GPU texture size (KF tiles to wall-sized), SA covers Mandelbrot
+ Multibrot 3–5 only, no `.map` palette import yet (blocked on sample files), 3D explicitly out of
scope. The gradient editor, bookmarks, dual Julia, tours, `.fdn`/`.kfr` import and the export
pipeline are all present.

### F — (c) what is substantively new — the pitch

The **adaptive iteration budget** (nobody else raises the pixel budget from live GPU feedback),
**Newton-Raphson zoom** onto nuclei with the atom-size estimate, the cursor-driven **dual Julia at
depth**, the **script/tour system** with per-keyframe budgets and chapters, and the **F3-matched
corpus** offered as evidence rather than a boast. Secondary but unusual: the app explains its own
rendering limits in the status bar instead of leaving a black screen unexplained.

### Explicitly deferred, named not hidden

The 1e95 depth wall (self-reporting), the glitch-correction pathology, the offline tour path's
unbounded per-frame cost and memory, the autopilot rework, the tour editor, and the proposals
backlog.

Living backlog. Specs: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md), [UI-DESIGN.md](UI-DESIGN.md).
Mockups: [design/mockups/](design/mockups/).

- [x] ✅⭐⭐**`--render-iter` DESTROYED ITS OWN PAYLOAD — fixed 2026-09-04.** "Export raw iteration
  data (EXR) instead of a colored image" wrote through `write_exr`, the COLOUR writer, whose
  `srgb_to_linear` **clamps to [0, 1]**. The R channel is the smooth iteration count — hundreds of
  thousands — so every pixel clamped to 1.0 and `srgb_to_linear(1.0) = 1.0` left the channel a
  **constant**. Measured before the fix on a 1e30× render: R was 1.0 at all 65,536 pixels,
  distinct-value count **1**. G/B (signed normals) were squashed into [0, 1] by the same clamp;
  only A (`log2` DE), the one channel the writer passes through untouched, survived. After:
  **62,100 distinct values**, normals back to −1..1.
  ⭐**A raw channel that reads back as a constant is indistinguishable from a renderer that
  computed nothing**, which is why this sat unnoticed in a feature whose whole purpose is
  cross-tool comparison. Fix = `write_exr_raw` (verbatim, no clamp, no transfer curve) used by
  `render_iter_to_file`; the three genuine colour exports keep `write_exr`, where the transform is
  correct and deliberate. Regression test `exr_raw_writes_data_verbatim_including_out_of_range_values`
  is mutation-verified: point it at `write_exr` and it fails `value 0 changed: 1 != 600008`.
  ⚠This also means **any past `--render-iter` output is worthless** — and it is the intended
  instrument for the raw-channel EXR / zoomasm work and for F3 per-channel comparison, so those
  items were resting on a broken tool.

- [x] ⛔⭐**THE SMOOTH ITERATION COUNT IS AN ABSOLUTE f32, QUANTISED TO 16 LEVELS AT DEPTH —
  AND THE IMPACT IS MEASURED FALSE** (measured 2026-09-04, now that `--render-iter` works).
  `smit = f32(iter) + 1.0 - nu` goes into the iterate texture's R channel as an absolute value,
  and the palette position is `smit × cycle + offset`. f32 has a 24-bit significand, so the
  fractional resolution collapses as the count grows. Corpus location **15 (3.7e163, 1,600,000
  iteration cap)**, rendered 192×192 `--ss 1`:

  | magnitude band | pixels | f32 ulp | distinct fractional values |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 5e5 – 1e6 | 26,619 | 0.0625 | **16** |
  | 1e6 – 2e6 | 10,198 | 0.125 | **16** |

  Every escaped pixel there lies between 890,252 and 1,599,980 — the whole image sits in the band
  where the fraction has 16 steps. (`aux_pack` takes `frac` but only to blend the stripe/TIA
  averages, so `smit` is the sole carrier of position.) Exactly at `--iter 10000000`, which the
  selftest pins as honoured verbatim, ulp reaches 1.0 and the fraction is gone entirely —
  smooth colouring is then arithmetically impossible.
  ⛔⭐⭐**IMPACT MEASURED FALSE 2026-09-05 — the arithmetic is real, the consequence is not, and
  this should NOT be "fixed".** The visual question is settled by one number: **how far a
  quantisation step spans on screen**, i.e. the SPATIAL gradient of `smit`. Measured on the same
  loc-15 dump:

  | | |δsmit| between adjacent pixels |
  |---|---|
  | 1st percentile | 26.5 |
  | median | 744 |
  | 99th percentile | 321,007 |
  | **smoothest 16×16 patch in the frame** | **71.3** |

  The quantisation step there is **0.125**. Even in the smoothest patch the field moves **570×
  further per pixel** than one step, and at the 1st percentile still 212×. A plateau needs at
  least a pixel to be seen; these are ~0.002 px wide. **There is no room for a band.**
  ⭐The regime that could revive it needs |δsmit| per pixel to approach 0.1 *while* `smit` sits at
  ~1e6 — and those fight each other: reaching a million iterations means hugging the boundary,
  which is exactly where the field is steepest. At this location the colouring is limited by
  ALIASING (744 iterations between neighbours — the confetti/Nyquist regime `--normalize` and the
  log scale exist for), not by f32.
  ⛔**Deliberately not applying the relative-base fix.** It has no measured benefit, and this repo
  has already paid for that once: the mode-0 rebase-underflow "fix" was equally well-argued, also
  had no measured impact, and drifted three determinism checks. Left recorded so the next person
  finds the measurement instead of re-deriving the arithmetic.
  ⭐**The fix is cheap and needs no wider texture**: store `smit` RELATIVE to a per-frame base
  (the frame already tracks its escape range via `esc_range_commit`) instead of absolutely. A
  frame spanning 890k–1.6M has ~710k of dynamic range, which f32 resolves to ~7 decimal digits —
  the problem disappears because it was never about range, only about offset.
  Method, to reproduce: `--render-iter -o x.exr --center <loc 15> --zoom 3.7e163 --iter 1600000
  --size 192x192 --ss 1`, then read the R channel and count `unique(v - floor(v))` per magnitude
  band.

- [x] ✅⭐⭐**DONE beta.132 — the prefetch prices the SUCCESSOR, and every one is now consumed.**

- [x] ✅⭐⭐**FIXED beta.147 — A SERIES-APPROXIMATION SKIP PAST THE ITERATION BUDGET RENDERS THE
  WHOLE FRAME BLACK. Field report 2026-08-25: dual view at 6.2e39×, "Auto-scale iterations with
  zoom" toggled, and the Mandelbrot pane went solid black.**

  ⭐**The reporter's own Performance panel carries the proof**: `SA skip 266,796` against
  `eff iter 224,000` — the skip is PAST the entire budget. The shader seeds `iter = iu.sa_skip`
  and then runs `loop { if (iter >= iu.max_iter) { break; } … }`, so the loop breaks on entry,
  every pixel exits with `iter >= max_iter`, is classified max-iter-exhausted, and colours as
  INTERIOR. The frame is black by construction.

  ⭐**Why toggling auto-scale triggers it**: the skip is computed against the REFERENCE's orbit
  length (`series_skip(.., orbit_iter, ..)`), never against the frame's budget. Auto-scale dropped
  the budget to 224,000 while the cached reference still carried a 266,796 skip, inverting the two.
  Any change that lowers the budget without rebuilding the reference can do this.

  **Fix**: `usable_sa_skip(skip, max_iter)` — REFUSE the skip when `skip >= max_iter` (both the
  live and the export request sites). ⭐**Refusing is correct, not a degradation**: the frame then
  iterates 0..max_iter the ordinary way and produces the right image, just more slowly. ⛔**Clamping
  would be WRONG** — the SA coefficients describe the orbit AT `skip`, so a truncated skip seeds
  the wrong state.

  ⭐**Demonstrated end to end, both directions**, by forcing `skip = 300,000` against `iter =
  224,000` at a deep view:

  | | mean luminance | black pixels |
  |---|---|---|
  | guard bypassed | 6.15 | **99.6%** |
  | guard on | **148.52** | **0.0%** |

  **Gates**: selftest 139/139 + 18/18, unit green (incl. a new `sa_skip_budget` case pinning
  refuse-don't-clamp at the exact 266,796/224,000 numbers), livetest 24/24 · 0 drifted, motiontest
  PASS, corpus 38/38.

  a mid-settle frame the user caught in passing.

  ⭐⭐**RULED OUT — it is NOT a colour-mapping artefact, so do not start with normalize.** The
  obvious theory is that tiles were coloured under different normalized palette mappings (which is
  a real open item, see the entry below). It cannot be that: the **iterate** pass is scissored to
  the tile (`set_scissor_rect`, gpu/lib.rs ≈1702) but the **colour** pass is NOT — it redraws the
  whole frame every time, from one set of colour uniforms. A global mapping cannot produce a
  rectangular seam. So the blocks are **stale ITERATION DATA**: regions of the iteration texture
  holding escape values computed for a DIFFERENT view and never re-iterated.

  **Where to look**, given that:
  • The pan path REPROJECTS — it translates the existing texture and fills the newly revealed
    border with the average colour — and only re-iterates afterwards. A revealed strip that never
    gets re-iterated is exactly a block of wrong content, and the vertical sliver at the pane edge
    has the shape of a revealed strip.
  • The tiled settle composes into that same texture one tile per frame. A grid that completes
    (or is torn down) before covering the reprojected region leaves the rest holding old data.
    `tile_state[vidx]` is dropped when `!can_tile && !will_reproject`, and re-armed on a key
    change — the interaction between "still reprojecting", "grid complete" and "key unchanged" is
    the suspect region.
  • ⚠Note the adjacent fix of 2026-08-30: `settings_hash` was missing `formula`/`julia`, so a
    completed grid could hold a texture computed for another FORMULA. That was the same class —
    the settle key failing to notice the texture is stale — and it is worth checking whether the
    key is also blind to whatever a pan changes here.

  ⚠**Intermittent** ("sometimes"), so a reproduction is the first job, not a fix. `--motiontest`
  and `--resizetest` drive motion but neither asserts anything about a settled frame's
  UNIFORMITY; a check would want to pan, let it settle, and require no rectangular discontinuity
  (a column/row-wise gradient scan finds a straight edge that a whole-frame stddev cannot).

  ⛔Do not confuse this with the RESOLVED deep-settle pixellation item further down: that was the
  whole frame rendered at a shrunken resolution and upscaled (uniformly blocky). This is
  full-resolution content that is simply WRONG in rectangles.~~

  ✅RESOLVED v0.2.41-beta.11 — the wall clock is GONE; the loop is bounded in WORK.**
  `CorrectionBudget { cpu_bits2, gpu_steps }` replaces the `Instant` deadline end to end: the CPU
  half prices every reference build (the FRONT build included — the 387 s half of the defect) in
  steps×bits², the GPU half prices every correction pass in nominal steps, and both are
  ADMISSION-priced — a build or pass that would exceed its half never starts, so the cut point is
  a function of the request alone. The per-pass price is `glitch_build_price`, shared with the
  selftest so the check can never drift from the loop. The base render is deliberately NOT priced:
  declining it saves nothing (the fallback renders the same frame uncorrected) and nominal steps
  overprice a BLA/SA-skipping deep frame by orders of magnitude (the e4000 base measured 0.58 s).
  `GLITCH_CPU_BUDGET` (3e14) / `GLITCH_GPU_BUDGET` (4e12) restate the old 120 s responsiveness
  intent in deterministic currency — the budget was NOT raised, per the warning below. Pinned by a
  new selftest check (D2e, 169th): the seahorse scene run twice under a budget sized to front + 1
  pass cuts at 2 refs BOTH runs, bit-identical, against 7 unbounded — the budget engages, so the
  check can go red. End-to-end: two `--render --glitch` runs at seahorse 1e8× (refs=64, 63
  correction passes each) compare 0/589,824 pixels differ by decoded RGB. Suite 346, selftest
  169/169 + 18/18, warning-free.** The rug
  investigation's `--no-glitch` A/B pinned it: with correction off, e4000 renders are
  byte-identical across runs AND across backends; with it on, the same binary's two runs differ
  (3–101 bytes, counters swinging 5%) because the wall-clock budget cuts the pass loop at a
  load-dependent point. A determinism contract (the corpus check, the goldens) cannot include a
  wall-clock-bounded stage at depths where the budget binds — bound it in WORK (passes/steps), or
  exclude corrected output from byte-comparisons past the depth where the deadline bites.**
  `GLITCH_CORRECT_BUDGET` is 120 s and bounds the tiled correction loop — but not the reference
  build that precedes it. At 2.37e4000× that build takes **387 s**, so the budget is three times
  blown before the first tile, the whole pass is discarded, and the frame renders from the base
  reference anyway.

  ⭐Until `f21683f` that meant 387 s spent purely to throw away; the correction pass now clones the
  caller's reference, so the waste is gone at this depth. **The deadline is still wrong though** —
  it just no longer has a 387-second build to be wrong about. Any path that *does* have to build
  (no request to clone: the selftest call, or a future caller) hits the same thing.

  ⇒ Either check the deadline before starting a build that cannot finish inside it, or price the
  build into the budget so the decision to attempt correction is made with the real cost in view.

  ⚠**Do not simply raise the budget.** 120 s is a responsiveness contract for an interactive
  export; the problem is that the expensive half is outside the thing measuring it.

- [x] 🟡**`minimap-pan-redraws` PRODUCED A FALSE RED UNDER MACHINE LOAD (2026-08-31).
  ✅RESOLVED v0.2.41-beta.13 — the measurement was quieted; the 9.5 gate stands untouched.**
  The race: a cleared pending flag is NOT "fully resolved" — the AA ramp advances only between
  grids, so the frame a grid drains, both pending flags read false while the next, SHARPER
  stage has not yet dispatched (it re-arms one frame later). A capture firing in that gap lands
  on a mid-ramp frame (ss=1 vs the other step's ss=2 ≈ the observed 9.9); machine load WIDENS
  the gap, it does not create it. Fix (uitest harness only): "resolved" now also requires the
  AA ramp at target on every rendered view, and the whole busy-condition must hold quiet for
  350 ms before capture (the reference gate's own lesson), still bounded by the hard cap.
  Verified: 1 idle + 3 runs under a deliberate 24-worker CPU burn — 35/35 each, minimap-pan
  meanD **0.0 (tiled asserted)** all four; the old fixed population's 0.0–2.2 spread collapsed
  to flat zero. One run read
  **meanΔ 9.9** against a 9.5 gate and failed; two immediate re-runs of the SAME binary passed
  (34/34). The machine was busy — a release build and the user's own app running — and the change
  under test was in the Misiurewicz detector, which that check does not touch.

  The calibration sample was `fixed: 0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 2.2` vs `broken: 40.1, 43.0`. The fixed
  population is therefore WIDER than it was measured to be: 9.9 belongs to it.

  ⛔**Do not raise the gate to 20.** The check's own comment states the rule it was built on, and it
  is the right one: *"when a differential is noisy, quiet the measurement; never raise the threshold
  until the check can no longer fail."* A gate at 20 would still discriminate against 40+, but it
  would be absorbing noise instead of removing it, and the noise is a real settle race that could
  one day exceed 20 as well.

  ⭐**The remedy is a firmer settle wait before the capture**, not a wider gate. The step already
  gates on settle completion; the residual is the capture racing the last tiles under load. Worth
  checking whether the wait can block on the tile grid being fully resolved rather than on a
  frame-count or time cap.

  ⚠A gate that cries wolf is worse than no gate — it trains the reader to re-run until green, which
  is exactly what I did here. Verified it was flake (two clean re-runs) rather than assumed it.

  from a view, `find_misiurewicz` solves it in log magnification to any depth the ask names
  (`SolveScale`), and `misiurewicz_multiplier` gives λ — whose |λ| is the ZOOM PERIOD (the view
  repeats every log₂|λ| octaves) and whose arg is the twist per repeat. That last one is what makes
  a browser worth building: it can say, before you go, *what diving here will look like*.

  point's own feature scale — since a Misiurewicz point only looks like anything at the depth where

  `z_{k+p} − z_k` has degree 2^(k+p−1), and the number of parameters of exactly type (k,p) is
  ~2^(k+p−2) — verified exactly (integer polynomial arithmetic) as `2^(k−1) − 1` for p = 1, checked
  k = 2…8. So (2,1) is genuinely unique (c = −2), (16,1) has 32,767 of them, and (95,1) has ~2e28.
  ⇒ **A picker keyed on (k,p) alone is meaningless above tiny k.** Each gallery entry has to carry
  a SEED (or the solved coordinate itself), because the seed is what selects the root. Store the
  points, not the pairs.

  and it is **degenerate**: `l2d` grows monotonically along the orbit, so the minimum is always the
  orbit's LAST INDEX. It is not a criterion, it is "take the end of the orbit".

  ⭐⭐**And it looked like a clean sweep**: 0.0002 / 0.0167 / 0.1034 view-widths at e40 / 283k× /
  e89 — beating the shipped ranking at all three locations at once. The reason it flattered itself
  is the trap: **"the solve lands near the centre" does NOT validate a (k,p)**. At depth Newton's
  basin converges to a nearby point for almost any pair — measured, k = 16 … 3900 all reach the
  SAME root at e40. Judge a ranking on whether the PAIR is right, never on where the solve ends up.

  ⚠Detection at e40 now costs **~1.5 s** (46 ms at e89 and 283k×): the looser, correct filter admits
  more candidates for the bignum ranking to sift. Off-thread with a spinner and a Cancel, so it is
  paid for — but a scale window in the pre-filter would cut it if it ever bites.

  `z_{k′+p} = z_{k′}` holds for all of them and each is a valid equation for the same root. The
  ranking already reduces the PERIOD to its fundamental (harmonics: if (k,p) fits so does (k,2p)) —
  the symmetric reduction for the PRE-PERIOD was never written. Which pair wins currently depends
  on how many candidates the pre-filter admits: I measured the reported k rising 33 → 95 → 159 as
  the threshold was loosened 4× → 16× → 64× the view span.

  found, so the user is told the feature is (95,1). Navigation is unaffected — same point.

  ⚠**Do NOT just take the smallest k from the candidate list.** The scale-aware ranking exists
  because the closest-separation pair at depth is routinely a *different, coarser* point — (437,3)
  at the e89 dendrite, 3.7e12 view-widths out. The reduction has to hold p FIXED and walk k down
  only while the near-return stays within the winner's own slack, exactly as the period reduction
  does. `detecting_at_the_view_scale_finds_a_pair_that_solves_here` is the gate to watch: if the
  reduction ever changes which POINT is found, it has gone wrong.

  caught: the acceptance must be scale-RELATIVE (`log2(sep) − log2|D_k|`, the tail-invariant the
  pre-filter already ranks by), not the harmonics' absolute slack — the absolute form admitted
  garbage at early k′ where |D| is tiny and reduced one deep view's winner to (1,1), which does
  not even Newton-converge. Pinned by an antenna-tip regression ((31,1) → (2,1) at −2+1e−20).

  Newton-solve to the same point, Δ ≈ 2^−95 view-widths); the deep test now asserts the
  canonical shape.

- [x] 🟠**THE NORMALIZED PALETTE MAPPING MOVES WHILE THE IMAGE IS STILL RESOLVING, AND AGAIN
  BETWEEN FRAMES OF A SEQUENCE (user, 2026-08-29). ✅RESOLVED — sequence half beta.8, live
  half beta.9.** It should be decided once and HELD: stable
  while a single view refines, and stable across every frame of a rendered sequence.

  **What the user sees**: colours shift under them as a deep view settles — the picture is
  re-mapped, not just sharpened — which is jarring in a way a sharpening image is not.

  ⭐**Both halves already have an EMA. Neither is a HOLD, and that is the point of this item** —
  do not "add smoothing", it is there:
  • **Live**: `norm_window_feed` (render.rs) accumulates min-min/max-max while a progression is
    mid-walk and feeds the EMA **once per completed walk**, at α = 0.3. So a refine that completes
    several walks moves the mapping in a few visible steps (three feeds ≈ 66% of the way to the
    new range). Smoothed, not held.
  • **Offline sequences**: `render_export_normalized`'s `prev_smoothed`, α = 0.2, threaded through
    the tour loop as `norm_range` (scripting.rs ≈ 3558/3766/3773). Also a lag, not a lock.

  ⚠**A refine genuinely CHANGES the measured range, so a chaser will always chase.** The coarse
  pass samples fewer pixels and therefore measures a NARROWER escape range than the finished
  frame; the mapping is being recomputed from a moving measurement. Holding the first reading is
  therefore not obviously right either — the first reading is the least representative one. This
  is the design question the item has to answer, not a bug with an obvious patch.

  **Three ways the sequence half breaks today, all read off the code rather than supposed:**
  1. **`--order progressive` already warns about it** (scripting.rs ≈ 3594): the EMA follows
     RENDER order, and bisection renders time-adjacent frames far apart, so the assembled video
     shimmers at refinement boundaries. The warning tells the user to re-render sequentially —
     which is a workaround standing in for this fix.
  2. **`--resume` restarts the EMA cold.** The resume path `continue`s on a frame already on disk
     (≈ 3648) BEFORE any feed, so frames rendered after an interruption are mapped from a history
     that skipped everything already written. The seam lands mid-video.
  3. **A sharded render has one EMA per shard.** `segment_range` splits a render across machines
     and each process starts at `norm_range = None`, so every shard boundary is a potential
     mapping change.

  ⭐**What "stable" probably has to mean**: a range keyed to the VIEW rather than to the render —
  computed once for a frame (or interpolated along the tour's own time axis from the keyframes'
  ranges) and then applied identically no matter what order, on what machine, or in how many
  passes the frame gets rendered. The progressive warning already names the shape of it:
  "time-keyed normalize ranges would lift this".

  ⚠**Whatever lands must be checked against the live path AND a sequence**, and the live half is
  the one with the trap: an offline A/B says nothing about it, because a CLI render never
  normalizes without `--normalize` (see the live-normalization notes). The existing
  `normalize-reduces-speckle` selftest check compares mappings, not their stability — a new check
  has to render the SAME view twice at different refinement states and require the mapping out.

  ✅**SEQUENCE HALF RESOLVED v0.2.41-beta.8** — exactly the "time-keyed normalize ranges" shape
  the progressive warning named: one canonical measuring pass per keyframe view (fixed 480×270,
  the keyframe's own iteration budget) anchors (t, range) points; every frame applies the
  piecewise-linear interpolation at its own tour time (`norm_anchor_range` +
  `NormRange::Fixed`). All three named breaks close at once — MEASURED, not argued: pre-fix,
  sequential vs `--order progressive` on a 2-keyframe probe differed on 5 of 6 frames (maxΔ up
  to 247/255, 97% of pixels); post-fix, sequential vs progressive vs a
  delete-3-frames-`--resume` run are maxΔ 0.000000 on every frame. Bonuses that fell out: the
  mapping is now output-size-independent (720p preview = 4K final palette), an all-interior
  mid-tour frame keeps the sequence mapping instead of silently flipping un-normalized for one
  frame, and the progressive+normalize warning is lifted. Cross-GPU sharding still differs where
  cross-vendor floats do — the global caveat, not a normalize one. The render-order EMA survives
  only as the fallback when no anchor measures (all-interior tour). Single `--render --normalize`
  is byte-identical to before (`NormRange::OwnFrame`).

  ✅**LIVE HALF RESOLVED v0.2.41-beta.9** — the design question answered the same way as the
  offline half: decide from the VIEW. `norm_feed_decision` (pure, unit-pinned): motion CHASES
  with the α=0.3 EMA exactly as before (a dive's mapping glides); the first settled reading of
  a new view signature ADOPTS the whole-frame reading OUTRIGHT (α=1 — one 0.3 feed would hold
  a mapping still 70% at the previous view; the settled full-res reading is exactly what the
  offline anchors measure); every further reading at that signature is HELD, so ss-ramp
  stages, settle tiles and chunked-walk refreshes stop re-mapping the picture. The signature =
  centre + depth + iteration ask (a budget raise extends real escapes — re-deciding there is
  honest). ⭐Engagement proven, not assumed: livetest and `--shot` turned out to never deliver
  norm readings at all (their loops idle the readback pump — a pass there is VACUOUS for this
  feature); a windowed `--autodive 8` with `FRACTADYNE_TRACE=gpu` showed all three states
  live: 13 Chase / 2 Adopt / 10 Hold. Grand-tour livetest 24/24, 0 drift (the un-normalized
  live path is untouched); suite 346; selftest 168/168 + 18/18. Remaining eye-check: a deep
  normalized settle in the GUI should now sharpen without re-colouring — the original report's
  own scenario.

  STARVED view sits in (`chunk=[35733,35733)`). The adaptive iteration budget reads that counter to
  decide whether to raise, so it saw **`frac = 0.0000` on a frame where 100% of pixels were capped**

  the counters) removes the race instead of recovering from it. The "norm hold BROKEN"
  trace line names any occurrence in the field meanwhile.

  ```
  +170.237s  LETHAL-BAND FRAME: gpu_iterate=1113ms  steps=5.622e10 budget=7.389e10 -> retreat 2.020e10
  +232.408s  LETHAL-BAND FRAME: wall_iterate=1216ms steps=1.648e9  budget=3.935e10 -> retreat 5.420e8
  +232.587s  DEVICE LOST (Unknown)
  ```
  `manifest: LIVE view=0 mode=0 1460x1102 ss=1 iter=231676 (gpu_iter=231676, eff=2000000,
  boost=16.78) steps=1.648e9 chunk=[768,1792) budget=5.420e8 tile=false orbit_len=111885
  partial=false settled=true since_mode_switch=3355 frames`, uptime 232.6 s, lost in `Queue::submit`.

  ⭐⭐**THE FATAL FRAME WAS 24x UNDER BUDGET AND STILL TOOK 1216 ms.** `steps=1.648e9` against
  `budget=3.935e10`. That is the sharpest statement yet of the standing lesson — **nominal steps do
  not predict wall time** — and it says the controller cannot see this coming from its own metric.
  Compare the frame 62 s earlier: `steps=5.622e10` (34x MORE work) at `1113ms` (LESS time).
  ⭐**And the retreat could not save it.** It cut the budget 3.935e10 -> 5.420e8, but the frame that
  died still carried `steps=1.648e9` — **3x over the NEW budget** — and that frame was already
  sized. Same shape as the closed mode-2 HOME item, now reproduced in **mode 0** by a user simply
  zooming.

  ⛔⭐⭐**CORRECTION 2026-08-24 — "THE RETREAT HAS NO CODE PATH TO THE WINDOW SIZER" IS WRONG, AND
  SO IS "RESOLUTION IS ITS ONLY ACTUATOR" FOR THE CHUNKED CASE.** Read at `render.rs` ≈4187 the
  settled walk sizes a pass as **`budget_step.min(chunk_band_license(bands, band, floor))`**, and
  `budget_step = clamp(budget·pace / (px·ss²), 256, gpu_iter)` (`render.rs:4095`, floor
  `render.rs:4030`). So the budget DOES reach the window — through the `min`:

  | | budget | `budget_step` | licence | window run |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | fatal frame | 3.935e10 | **24,457** | 1024 | 1024 (licence bound) |
  | after the retreat | 5.420e8 | **337** | 1024 | **337** (budget_step binds) |

  The 24,457 reproduces this entry's own figure exactly, which is what validates the model. So the
  retreat would have cut the window **3×**, to ~337 iterations — comfortably out of the band, since
  1024 priced at ~1216 ms.
  ⭐⭐**THE DEFECT IS THEREFORE FEEDBACK LATENCY, NOT A MISSING ACTUATOR.** The lethal reading
  arrives ~2 frames after the dispatch it prices, so the dying frame had already been sized under
  the old budget. The actuator was adequate and simply arrived late. ⚠That reframes the fix away
  from "give the retreat an iteration-axis actuator" (it has one) and toward **acting sooner**:
  clamp `boost` on the frame after a lethal reading (this entry already suspected it), retreat on
  the WALL-clock accumulator (`chunk_pass_dt`) without waiting for the GPU timestamp, and consider
  whether `budget_step`'s 256 floor is itself too high on hostile regions.
  ✅⭐⭐**PARTIAL FIX beta.139 — THE RETREAT NOW SHEDS THE BAND LEDGER TOO.** With the diagnosis
  corrected, the one term the retreat genuinely could not reach is the EARNED LICENCE. It cuts the
  budget, and `budget_step` reaches the window through the `min` — but only while `budget_step` is
  the smaller term, and it floors at 256. The other term is `chunk_band_license`, and **nothing in
  the retreat path could lower it**.

  ⭐⭐**AND THE ORDINARY CLIFF RULE CANNOT BE RELIED ON TO SHED IT, WHICH IS THE REAL FIND.**
  `chunk_band_update` quarters a band on a price past 2× target, but it runs ONLY on a pass the
  walk judged DRAINED (`last_dt_ms < CHUNK_DRAIN_DT_MS` — the quick present, `render.rs`≈4051).
  A queue on its way to losing the device is saturated, quick presents stop, and the hot pass stays
  `chunk_inflight` — **unpriced**. So the single pass whose price would shed the licence is exactly
  the pass the release gate silences, and the band keeps a licence earned on this region's cheap
  frames. That is `chunk=[768,1792)` in the field log: a 1024-iteration window still sized by a
  licence, at a moment when nothing was being priced.

  **Fix**: `chunk_band_retreat(&mut perf.chunk_bands[v])` on a lethal reading — every band reopens
  at the floor, which is the ledger's own documented "first contact with ANY region, however
  hostile, is a survivable single".
  ⭐**Output-neutral by construction**: window size sets only where a pass stops and resumes, never
  what it computes (bit-identity for any `chunk_iters` is gated by the chunked selftests and
  `--chunk-sweep`'s pixel-identity assertion). The cost is throughput — the walk re-climbs from the
  floor in ~8 priced passes on the ×2 fast lane — and on a frame that came within ~2× of losing
  the device that is the right trade.
  ⚠**ALL bands, not the current one**: the reading is ~2 frames stale, so the band it refers to is
  no longer the band about to dispatch — shedding "the" band would shed the wrong one.

  **Gates**: selftest **139/139 + 17/17**, unit tests all green incl. a new
  `a_lethal_retreat_sheds_every_earned_license_back_to_the_floor`, **livetest 24/24 · 0 drifted**
  (real 331 s tour), **motiontest PASS**, **F3 corpus 38/38**, and a forced-lethal
  `--autodive 24 --set TDR_LETHAL_MS=1` run: exit 0, **196** lethal readings, **0** device losses
  or panics under continuous shedding.

  ⚠⚠**THIS DOES NOT CLOSE THE ITEM.** It removes one way a large window can survive a near-death,
  but the dying frame in this report was ALREADY SIZED and in flight — nothing acting at
  lethal-reading time can save that frame. The latency itself is untouched. **Still open**: retreat
  on the WALL accumulator without waiting for the drained-pass gate; whether `budget_step`'s 256
  floor is too high on hostile regions; and — ✅**FIXED beta.140, below** — `CHUNK_BANDS` granularity.

  ✅⭐⭐**FIX beta.140 — THE BANDS ARE OCTAVES FROM A FIXED BASE, NOT A FRACTION OF THE ASK.**
  The granularity question, and the arithmetic makes it the closest thing to a root cause yet. The
  index was `cur · CHUNK_BANDS / gpu_iter` — the ask cut into 16 equal parts — so **a band's width
  grew with the ask** and the ledger's resolution collapsed at exactly the depths where device
  losses happen:

  | | band width at the fatal ask (231,676) | band holding the fatal window `[768,1792)` |
  |---|---|---|
  | old (ask/16) | **14,480 iterations** | band 0 = `[0, 14480)` |
  | new (octaves from 256) | 512 iterations there | band 2 = `[512, 1024)` |

  Under the old rule that window's 1024-iteration licence had been earned by the passes at
  iterations **0..768 — the cheap start of the orbit**. Octaves make that impossible: a licence at
  band 2 can only have been earned inside `[512,1024)`. **28× finer attribution exactly where it
  mattered.**
  ⭐⭐**This is `chunk_band_license`'s own warning, one level up.** It already refuses to let
  UNVISITED territory inherit a neighbour's licence, because "a 36k-step pass earned on a band's
  cold beginning ran TEN SECONDS when the band turned hot mid-way — the storm starts before the
  wrap point, **INSIDE the band**". That bounded the gap BETWEEN bands; nothing bounded the gap
  WITHIN one, and a 14,480-iteration band has a great deal of "within".
  ⭐**Octaves, not fixed width**: cost structure along an orbit is scale-free (wrap points and
  storms sit at multiplicatively-spaced depths), and a fixed width fine enough for `cur = 768`
  would need thousands of bands to reach a 4M ask. 16 octaves from 256 cover `cur` to 4.2M.
  ⭐**Throughput is neutral-to-better, not worse** — the obvious worry is more floor-openings, but
  walking 0..231,676 crosses **11** octave bands against **16** equal ones (octaves compress the
  top), and the fine bands are tiny ranges at the very start (256/256/512 iterations) where
  reopening at the floor costs almost nothing.

  **Gates**: selftest **139/139 + 17/17**; unit tests green incl. two new cases — one pinning the
  octave boundaries, one that encodes the OLD rule inline to show it collapsed `cur=0` and
  `cur=768` into a single band while the new rule separates them; **livetest 24/24 · 0 drifted**
  (real 331 s tour); **motiontest PASS**; **F3 corpus 38/38**; forced-lethal
  `--autodive 24 --set TDR_LETHAL_MS=1` exit 0, **301** lethal readings, **0** device losses.

  ✅⭐⭐**FIX beta.141 — THE LEDGER NOW RETREATS ON THE WALL ACCUMULATOR, NO DRAIN REQUIRED.**
  Second lead closed. Until now the ledger learned NOTHING about an in-flight pass until it
  drained (`last_dt_ms < CHUNK_DRAIN_DT_MS` — a quick present as proof the queue emptied) or hit
  the wedge backstop, **and that backstop is `target × 60`, i.e. ~24 s at a 400 ms target** — long
  after a device would be gone. ⭐**That is the exact gap the field loss fell through**: a queue on
  its way to losing the device never produces a quick present, so the one pass whose price would
  shed the licence is precisely the pass that cannot be priced.

  **Fix**: accumulated wall is a conservative LOWER BOUND on what a pass has already cost — if
  `acc` reaches the lethal band the pass has *already* been that expensive, and no drain is needed
  to know it. Crossing it sheds the ledger (`chunk_band_retreat`), latched so a pass sitting in the
  band for many frames sheds once.
  ⚠**SHED, DO NOT RELEASE** — the next dispatch stays blocked until the genuine drain. "Releasing
  the next dispatch onto a pass that is merely SLOW is how a 10 s single got company on its way to
  the TDR"; that reasoning is untouched. This changes only what the NEXT pass may ask for.

  ⭐**VERIFIED FIRING, not merely written.** `--livetest` with `--set TDR_LETHAL_MS=1`:
  **46 sheds**, at octave bands 0/1/2, each reporting `size=256` (the floor), and the tour still
  **24/24 · 0 drifted**. ⚠⚠**Two earlier attempts did NOT reach the code and would have "passed"
  vacuously**: `--autodive 24` never chunks at all (`chunk_over` needs
  `spx·gpu_iter > tdr_steps`, and `--set TDR_LETHAL_MS` lowers the LETHAL threshold, not the
  budget — 0 `chunk=` lines), and `--autodive 34` chunks but stays INTERACTING, so every window is
  `chunk=[0,n)` restarting each frame and the settled in-flight path never runs. **A settled
  chunked walk needs the tour's holds.** ⚠This also qualifies the beta.139/140 gate runs: the
  forced-lethal autodives exercised the RETREAT, not the chunked walk.

  **Gates (stock, no overrides)**: selftest **139/139 + 17/17**, unit tests green, **livetest
  24/24 · 0 drifted**, **motiontest PASS**, **F3 corpus 38/38**.

  ✅⭐⭐**FIX beta.142 — THE `budget_step` FLOOR IS WALL-AWARE, AND THE "~70 ms" IT RESTED ON WAS
  STALE.** Third lead closed, and the stale figure is the finding.

  ⛔`chunk_band_license` justified the 256 floor with "~256 iterations is **~70 ms** even at the
  worst rate ever measured on this hardware". **The field loss ran 1024 iterations in 1216 ms —
  1.19 ms/iteration — so 256 there is ~304 ms** (~380 ms priced sub-linearly at the sweep's
  measured 1.79× per doubling). The quoted number was off by **4–5×**: survivable against the
  900 ms band by ~2.4×, not the ~13× it implied, and a region only **3× more hostile** makes the
  floor ITSELF lethal (900 / 256 = 3.5 ms per iteration).

  ⭐**The structural point**: `budget_step` is wall-derived (a measured step budget ÷ pixels), so
  the controller already sizes from evidence — right up until a fixed ITERATION floor overrides it,
  and it binds *precisely* when the measurement says "this region is hostile, go smaller".
  A fixed iteration count cannot bound wall time when cost per iteration varies by orders of
  magnitude between regions.

  **Fix**: floor = **min(256, what the worst measured rate says fits the target wall)**, using
  `mode_rate` (already kept as a running MINIMUM, i.e. pessimistic by construction).

  | ms/iteration | floor | floor's wall cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | 0.05 (benign) | 256 (unchanged) | 13 ms |
  | 1.19 (**the field loss**) | 256 (unchanged) | 304 ms |
  | 2.50 | 160 | 400 ms |
  | 3.52 (**old floor would be lethal**) | 113 | 398 ms |
  | 8.00 | 50 | 400 ms |

  ⚠**`min`, deliberately — it can only ever LOWER the floor.** In a benign region the computed
  value is orders of magnitude above 256 and nothing changes, so the blast radius is confined to
  regions whose own measurements say the old floor was too big. It can never raise the floor,
  enlarge a pass, or slow a healthy walk.
  ⚠⚠**THIS ONE CANNOT BE OBSERVED FIRING ON HEALTHY HARDWARE — BY DESIGN.** The valve engages only
  past ~1.03e6 steps/ms, just beyond the worst region ever observed here, so unlike the beta.141
  wall-retreat there is no run that shows it acting. It is verified by ARITHMETIC (table above) and
  by the gates showing it changes nothing where it should change nothing. ⭐Treat that as a weaker
  form of evidence than the 46 observed sheds, and say so.
  ⚠The band-licence floor in `chunk_band_license` stays a constant: an unvisited band has no
  measured rate of its own to size from — that is the whole point of it.

  **Gates (stock)**: selftest **139/139 + 17/17**, unit green, **livetest 24/24 · 0 drifted**,
  **motiontest PASS**, **F3 corpus 38/38**.

  🔴**WHAT REMAINS, and it is not a code change.** All three leads are now closed, and the item is
  still open for one reason: **a dispatch already in flight cannot be recalled.** Every fix here
  makes the NEXT pass smaller; none can save the frame that is already running, which is what
  killed the device. Bounding that requires never issuing a lethal window in the first place, and
  prediction from nominal steps is measured-false. ⭐**A reproduction is what would close this** —

  ⛔**A reproduction is still what would close it**, and this crash predates both the beta.135

  ⚠**`eff=2000000` with `boost=16.78`** — the adaptive budget had boosted a 2M ceiling hard. Worth

  ⚠**Instrumentation note**: the first lethal frame reports `gpu_iterate=`, the fatal one

  are not.** Same request, ss = 2, chunked vs unchunked, varying only `color_method`:

  |---|---|---|---|

  175.4 ms). ~21 ms to clear and store 4.2 MB of attachments is ~200 MB/s, roughly 100× too slow —

  | render target | total (219 windows) | worst window |
  |---|---|---|
  | 640×**483** (odd) | **5261 ms** | 46.0 ms |
  | 640×**482** (even) | **473 ms** | 4.4 ms |
  | 320×**241** (odd) | **4909 ms** | 43.8 ms |
  | 320×**240** (even) | **193 ms** | 3.2 ms |

  ⭐**One pixel row, 11×. Perfectly correlated across eight samples**: every even height is
  monotonic in area, every odd height sits at ~5 s regardless of size (483, 241 and 121 all land
  within 8% of each other while spanning 16× in pixels). Same view, same reference, same window
  size, SA off on both arms — the ONLY difference is the parity of `height`.

  DIVIDE (`(resolution[1] as f64 * f) as u32`, `render.rs` ≈3872) and from `res_scale`, so odd
  heights are not an edge case — they are roughly half of all frames. If this reproduces on the live
  chunked path it is a ~25× cost multiplier switching on and off as the budget walks, which would
  by itself explain a rate "collapse" the controller cannot predict from nominal steps, and it is a
  candidate for the 62× per-step swing in the 2026-08-22 field log.

  ✅⭐⭐**MEASURED 2026-08-23 — IT IS PARITY, IT IS THE CHUNKED PATH ONLY, AND THE PENALTY GROWS AS
  THE TARGET SHRINKS.** New **height axis** in `--chunk-sweep` (`chunksweep.rs`): sweeps h-4..h+4
  around three height scales, each height run BOTH chunked (`render_iter_chunked_timed`) and
  unchunked (`render_iter`) as a control. Raw run in `local/sweep-height.log`, view 2^45.52,
  1280 wide, window 256, bracket [0,8192) = 32 windows.

  | height scale | even mean | odd mean | ratio | unchunked control |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | ~1102 | 277.1 ms | 410.1 ms | **1.48×** | 314–330 ms, FLAT |
  | ~551 | 147.8 ms | 264.4 ms | **1.79×** | 168–176 ms, FLAT |
  | ~275 | 78.4 ms | 192.0 ms | **2.45×** | 95–101 ms, FLAT |

  ⭐**PARITY, not alignment.** `h%4==0` (1100, 548, 276) and `h%8==0` (1104, 552, 272) sit exactly
  with the plain even rows — there is no 4- or 8-boundary. Only odd/even separates them, and the
  separation is clean: at every scale EVERY odd row is slower than EVERY even row.
  ⭐⭐**THE UNCHUNKED CONTROL IS FLAT**, which is the question this entry opened with: `render_iter`
  runs the same view as one dispatch with no ping-pong state textures and shows no parity ordering
  at any scale. **So it is the chunk path's state targets, and the iterate shader is exonerated.**
  ⭐**At the smallest scale, chunking an ODD-height target is SLOWER THAN NOT CHUNKING AT ALL**
  (192 ms chunked vs 97 ms unchunked) — the bound costs more than the work it bounds.

  ✅⭐⭐**FULLY REPRODUCED at the original geometry (219-window bracket, width scaled with height).**
  The 2.45× above was an artefact of a SHORT bracket (32 windows) and a fixed 1280 width; both
  predictions held.

  | target | even | odd | ratio | filed 2026-08-22 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1280 wide | 1926–1965 ms | 6935–8824 ms | **4.0×** | — |
  | 640 wide | 514–525 ms | 5019–5436 ms | **10.1×** | 640×482 = 473 ms / 640×483 = 5261 ms |
  | 320 wide | 207–222 ms | 4612–4648 ms | **21.6×** | 320×240 = 193 ms / 320×241 = 4909 ms |

  ⭐⭐**THE MECHANISM CLUE: the ODD cost is nearly AREA-INDEPENDENT.** Even heights scale with
  pixels (1950 → 519 → 213 ms, ~4× per halving, as they must). Odd heights barely move:

- [ ] 🟢**Offline render: order frames by DECREASING MAGNIFICATION and reuse one reference across
  them.** User idea 2026-08-18 ("render the deepest frame first and work backwards"), sharpened.
  ⭐**Why it works:** the orbit is ZOOM-INDEPENDENT (`Z_{n+1} = Z_n² + C_ref` depends only on centre
  and precision), and both live reuse gates are satisfied monotonically as you zoom OUT —
  `reuse.prec >= inp.precision` (the deepest frame has the maximum precision requirement, so it covers
  every shallower one) and drift `|dx|/span <= REUSE_MAX_DRIFT` (0.7; span grows, so the ratio shrinks,
  and in a zoom-in tour the deep target is CONTAINED in every earlier wider frame at ~0.5 or less).
  Surplus orbit length costs nothing — shallow frames simply iterate fewer samples of a buffer that is
  already resident, which is "truncation" obtained for free.
  ⚠**Order by decreasing magnification, NOT reverse timeline.** They coincide only for a monotonic
  dive. `tours/announce-4k.toml` has five chapters with hard cuts at different depths, where
  reverse-timeline order repeatedly returns to depth and breaks the precision gate. Sorting on
  magnification makes the gate unfailable by construction.
  ⚠⚠**THE BLOCKER: the offline path has NO reuse.** `scripting.rs:3556` PIPELINES instead — it starts
  frame N+1's `spawn_export_reference` while frame N renders ("the next frame IN RENDER ORDER"). So
  every frame still pays a full bignum build; the cost is only hidden behind the render, and at extreme
  depth (where the build alone is minutes) the build IS the critical path and hiding stops working.
  **Reverse ordering alone therefore buys nothing** — the work is wiring the live path's proven
  `try_reuse_reference` into the offline renderer. Together they replace N full builds with 1 build +
  N-1 extends, plausibly the largest offline throughput win available on deep tours.
  ⚠Caveats: the BLA tree still rebuilds every frame regardless of order (`dc_max` changes per frame —
  see T2c, which is the structural answer); the drift gate still resets at chapter cuts that pan far,
  so reuse holds WITHIN a dive, not across a whole multi-chapter tour; and it collides with
  `--order progressive` — deepest-first also gives the early look at deep frames that progressive was
  added for (arguably a better one, since it renders the most expensive and most failure-prone frame
  first), but bisection spreads early frames across the whole timeline and so catches problems anywhere.
  A new order needs the same permutation property tests `progressive_frame_order` now has, and ETA
  estimates will skew (expensive frames first).

    quasi-conformal pattern — compute once, finish millions of pixels. Largest potential constant-factor
    win at deep minibrot holds and **unusually GPU-friendly for us**: the mipmap is literally a texture,
    sampling belongs in a fragment shader, and we already carry the floatexp `D` per pixel for DE
    lighting, which is exactly the LOD input. ⭐**Extra argument for it: those are the same frames the

  out at ~9% brightness, which on a mid-blue reads as black.

  pixel agree; the normal varies between ADJACENT PIXELS, not inside the tap block. So the average
  is confident and wrong-ish rather than short and uncertain. Reverted, not shipped.

  2.03 pt (~14× better than aa 1×), at the usual supersampling cost.

  legitimately ~1 → ~250,000 at this depth: a thin halo hugging the boundary escapes very late while
  the bulk of the exterior escapes in 1–50. Normalising LINEARLY across that compresses everything
  visible into a sliver of the palette. Escape counts near the boundary are heavy-tailed, so linear
  min/max normalisation collapses whenever the iteration ceiling is high relative to the depth — it
  was designed for deep fields, where the escaped range is narrow and high.

  drops the count to suit 1×.

  switch or blend to a log mapping automatically, since that is what the user would do by hand;
  (c) leave it and document. Prefer (b) as the cheap correct-feeling default, with (a) if a histogram
  lands for other reasons. ⚠Whatever is chosen must not perturb the deep-field case the feature
  exists for — gate it with a shallow AND a deep golden.

- [x] ✅✅**FIXED beta.109 — THE SETTLED WALK LOSES THE DEVICE NO MORE (four layers, one night)**. Original entry follows; resolution appended at the end. 🔴🔴~~THE SETTLED WALK STILL LOSES THE DEVICE AT A WRAP-STORM VIEW~~ — the residual above,

  re-computing was a walk that runs ~1 s/frame and never finishes.
  ⭐⭐**THE MECHANISM CHAIN, each link measured**:
  (1) the settled walk dispatches one budget-sized pass EVERY frame → back-to-back ~1 s
  submissions with zero idle (the beta.48 lethal profile);
  (2) saturation SILENCES THE SENSOR — iterate timestamps arm only "when nothing is in flight" —
  so the budget hears mostly cheap slices and GROWS (readings 4.6e10→5.9e10 while 1 s frames
  flowed unmeasured; NO lethal reading ever fired in the fatal sessions);
  (3) the ask's cost is REGIONAL, with a CLIFF at cur ≈ orbit_len (634,214 here) where pixels
  wrap the reference — a rebase-storm band ~10-70× the cold rate. Every repro death sat at
  cur ≈ 830k-900k (pre-mitigation) or in the 634k+ band (post);
  (4) with the swapchain 2-4 presents deep, entering the cliff puts SEVERAL full-size passes in
  flight before the first honest price can land — frames 96-99 of the final repro: four
  consecutive ~1 s singles, then loss.
  🔨**BUILT (settled-walk-only, all evidence-gated, all floor-guarded)**: a backpressure PACER
  (hold the last range — unchanged triple, GPU dedupes — until CHUNK_PACE_GAP frames since the
  last dispatch when dt > CHUNK_PACE_DT_MS); WALL-PRICE sizing (`chunk_step_factor`, pure + 4
  tests: next pass = budget × target/last-pass-wall-price, clamped [1/16, 1] — the signal
  timestamps can't starve); SLOW-START (`chunk_ok_step`: a pass may be ≤1.25× the largest step
  whose wall price was SEEN ≤ target; reset per progression); CLIFF-SHED (a price >2× target
  quarters the license) + DRAIN-WAIT (after a hot pass, dispatch only after a quick frame proves
  the queue drained). Net effect measured: survival 13 s → 25 s, sizes moderate at the crossing —
  **the device still dies inside the cliff's detection-latency window.**
  📐**THE STRUCTURAL FIX (next session)**: PRICE-SERIALIZED WALKING — never more than ONE
  unpriced pass in flight (dispatch pass k+1 only once pass k's wall price has been observed).
  Zero regression on healthy views (a quick pass's price arrives by the next frame anyway); at
  unknown-cost regions the walk advances at exactly the rate its prices arrive, so a cliff can
  cost at most ONE marginal single. Design it with the controller_props treatment (pure fn +
  property tests), and consider regional rate memory (the mode_rate MIN-latch precedent, keyed
  on cur-bands relative to orbit_len) so re-walks of the same ask price the storm band correctly
  from pass one. ⚠Until it lands: a settled minibrot interior at a multi-million explicit ask
  remains device-lethal on this hardware — the same view at ≤250k, or with auto-iter on, is fine.
  ⚠The pin (motion) dispatches per-frame too and shares the queue-depth exposure in principle;
  autodive passes today, but apply the same discipline there when this lands.
  ✅✅**RESOLVED beta.109 (2026-08-20, design/mode2-chunking.md §12).** Price-serialized walking
  landed (≤1 unpriced pass in flight; wall price = accumulated dts to a quick-frame drain proof;

  the final band [3.93M, 3.96M] of a [288k, 3.96M] true range) → everything below clamps → FLAT.
  Tail bands without escapes → an earlier wider window survived → noise (correct). Fix =
  `norm_window_feed` (pure + 4 tests): readings ACCUMULATE (min-min/max-max) while
  `chunk_cursor ∈ (0, ask)` and feed the EMA once, whole, on completion — bit-for-bit the
  pre-walk cadence for un-chunked frames. Verified live at the reporting view: one feed,
  `ema Some((288040, 3962684))`, full range. ⚠The same trap-shape to keep in mind for ANY
  per-frame GPU readback now that frames can be partial passes: `capped_frac` (already
  ask-tagged ✔), the AA probe (settled-only ✔), the iter boost (reads capped_frac ✔) — audited,
  all guarded; the norm sink was the one that wasn't.
